Safety is Non-Compositional:
A Formal Framework for Capability-Based AI Systems

Cosimo Spera ††thanks: Corresponding author. Minerva CQ, 16400 Lark Ave, Los Gatos, CA 95032, USA. cosimo@minervacq.com. The methods described in this paper are protected by provisional patent No.˜74871717: “Systems and Methods for Capability-Based Safety Verification in Modular AI Systems Using Directed Hypergraph Closure.” Affiliation: Minerva CQ, Los Gatos, CA 95032
March 2026
Abstract

Central result. This paper contains the first formal proof that safety is non-compositional in the presence of conjunctive capability dependencies: two agents each individually incapable of reaching any forbidden capability can, when combined, collectively reach a forbidden goal through an emergent conjunctive dependency. This result (Theorem 9.2) is tight—it cannot arise in pairwise graph models, only in systems with AND-semantics—and shows that component-level safety checks are structurally insufficient for modular agentic systems.

To prove and apply this result, we introduce a formal framework in which AI capability systems are modelled as directed hypergraphs, where a hyperedge ({u1,…,uk},{v})(\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}\},\{v\}) fires only when all of u1,…,uku_{1},\ldots,u_{k} are simultaneously present. Traditional capability graphs assume pairwise dependencies and cannot express this AND-semantics without introducing artificial conjunction nodes. We prove that capability graphs embed into capability hypergraphs as a strict special case (Lemma 5.1 and Corollary 5.2), and that planning reduces to a single fixed-point closure computation grounded in the Horn clause completeness theorem of van Emden and Kowalski (1976), with an O⁡(n+m⋅k)O(n+m\cdot k) worklist algorithm.

Beyond safety, the closure framework supports a formal theory of goal discovery. We prove the closure gain function is submodular (Theorem 8.5), yielding a (1−1/e)(1-1/e) greedy acquisition guarantee; establish P-completeness of emergent capability detection (Theorem 8.3) and coNP-completeness of minimal unsafe set membership (Theorem 9.5); and unify these results in the Safe Audit Surface Theorem (Theorem 10.1)—a polynomial-time-computable, formally certifiable account of every capability an agent can safely acquire from any given deployment configuration. We extend the framework in five further directions: a coalition safety criterion, incremental dynamic maintenance, PAC-learning sample complexity (O⁡(n2​k/ε)O(n^{2k}/\varepsilon) trajectories suffice), probabilistic hypergraphs with expected closure computable in O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk), and an adversarial robustness result (MinUnsafeAdd is NP-hard; single-edge check is polynomial; greedy defence achieves (1−1/e)(1-1/e) via submodularity).

Empirically, 42.6% of real multi-tool trajectories (ToolBench G3 and TaskBench DAG) contain conjunctive dependencies (95% CI: [39.4%, 45.8%]); the hypergraph planner produces zero AND-violations, as proved; the workflow baseline produces AND-violations on 38.2% of conjunctive instances on real asynchronous traces.

Keywords: AI safety; agentic systems; capability composition; directed hypergraphs; formal verification; PAC learning; submodular optimisation.

1 Introduction

1.1 The Central Result

Theorem 1.1 (Non-Compositionality of Safety, informal).

This paper contains the first formal proof that safety is non-compositional in the presence of conjunctive capability dependencies. Specifically, two agents each individually incapable of reaching any forbidden capability can, when their capabilities are combined, collectively reach a forbidden goal. This is not an artefact of adversarial design; it is a structural consequence of AND-semantics that is invisible to pairwise graph models. The result is tight: it requires exactly three capabilities, one conjunctive hyperedge, and cannot arise in any pairwise graph.

This result—proved formally as Theorem 9.2—settles a concern that has been articulated informally in the AI safety literature (Russell and Norvig, 2021) but never formally proved in the capability-composition setting. It implies that any system deploying component-level safety checks as its sole safety guarantee is structurally incomplete, independently of how carefully individual components are designed.

1.2 Context and Motivation

Modern AI systems are increasingly constructed as modular ecosystems of capabilities rather than monolithic algorithms: agentic architectures, tool-augmented language models, robotic control systems, and enterprise automation frameworks all achieve higher-level tasks by composing multiple capabilities. Traditional modelling represents these dependencies using directed graphs, where each edge encodes a single sufficient enabling relationship. This representation assumes that dependencies are pairwise.

Many real tasks, however, require the simultaneous availability of multiple prerequisites. The dependency

(intent understanding,user context,database access)⟶answer generation(\text{intent understanding},\ \text{user context},\ \text{database access})\longrightarrow\text{answer generation}

cannot be represented in a directed graph without introducing artificial conjunction nodes—vertices representing logical conjunctions rather than genuine system capabilities. This is not a modelling inconvenience: it is the precise source of the safety failure. Two agents holding {u1}\{u_{1}\} and {u2}\{u_{2}\} individually appear safe. When combined, the conjunctive hyperedge ({u1,u2},{f})(\{u_{1},u_{2}\},\{f\}) fires, reaching forbidden goal ff. No pairwise graph model can represent—or detect—this.

Directed hypergraphs provide the natural remedy. A hyperedge connects a set of source vertices to a set of target vertices, directly expressing AND-semantics without artificial intermediate nodes. Section 4 develops a concrete running example—booking a trip to Paris—that grounds the abstract framework; the real empirical validation over 900 trajectories from public benchmarks is presented in Section 15.

1.3 Contributions

  1. 1.

    Non-compositionality of safety (Theorem 9.2). The first formal proof that the safe region ℛ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}(F) is not closed under union. The counterexample is minimal and the result is tight: it cannot arise in pairwise graph models.

  2. 2.

    Safe Audit Surface Theorem (Theorem 10.1). The paper’s primary deliverable: a polynomial-time-computable, formally certifiable map of every capability an agent can safely acquire, every capability one step beyond its current reach, and every capability it can never safely acquire.

  3. 3.

    Lattice structure of the safe region (Theorem 9.4). The safe region is a lower set in the power-set lattice; its boundary is a finite antichain of minimal unsafe sets, enabling one-time offline preprocessing for online safety checking.

  4. 4.

    Matching complexity bounds (Theorems 8.3 and 9.5). P-completeness of emergent capability detection and coNP-completeness of minimal unsafe set membership, establishing tight upper and lower bounds for the safety audit problem.

  5. 5.

    Empirical validation (Section 15). Across 900 real trajectories, 42.6% contain at least one conjunctive dependency (95% CI: [39.4%, 45.8%]); the hypergraph planner produces zero AND-violations on all traces (proved); the workflow baseline produces AND-violations on 38.2% of conjunctive instances on real asynchronous traces (95% CI: [33.4%, 43.1%]).

  6. 6.

    Graph embedding (Lemma 5.1 and Corollary 5.2). Capability graphs embed into capability hypergraphs as a strict special case, with exhaustive characterisation of the expressive gap.

  7. 7.

    Planning theorem (Theorem 6.3). Goal reachability reduces to a single closure computation, grounded in van Emden–Kowalski Horn clause completeness, with fully explicit plan construction in both directions.

  8. 8.

    Submodularity and greedy acquisition (Theorem 8.5 and Corollary 8.6). The closure gain function is submodular via the polymatroid rank theorem, with verified NWF78 preconditions and a (1−1/e)(1-1/e) greedy guarantee.

  9. 9.

    Goal discovery structure (Proposition 8.2). A consolidated characterisation of emergent capabilities, the near-miss frontier, and acquisition distance as a single proposition with four parts.

  10. 10.

    Coalition safety criterion (Theorem 11.2 and Corollary 11.4). A complete characterisation of nn-agent coalition safety: a coalition is unsafe if and only if the joint capability set covers some element of the minimal unsafe antichain ℬ⁡(F)\mathcal{B}(F), reducing online coalition monitoring to a linear-time set-cover query against a precomputed offline structure.

  11. 11.

    Dynamic hypergraph theorems (Theorems 11.6 and 11.7). Incremental closure maintenance under hyperedge insertion and deletion, with O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk) worst-case update cost, O⁡(|S|)O(|S|) lazy cost when the new edge does not immediately fire, and |T||T|-bounded acquisition distance stability.

  12. 12.

    PAC-learning sample complexity (Theorem 14.2). A VC-dimension bound establishing that O⁡(n2​k+ln⁡(1/δ)ε)O\!\left(\tfrac{n^{2k}+\ln(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right) trajectories suffice to learn the hyperedge structure to ε\varepsilon-error with confidence 1−δ1-\delta.

  13. 13.

    Probabilistic closure and non-compositionality (Theorem 14.5). Extension to probabilistic hypergraphs where each hyperarc fires with probability p⁡(e)p(e). Expected reachability is computable in O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk); non-compositionality persists for all thresholds τ<p⁡(h)\tau<p(h).

  14. 14.

    Adversarial robustness (Theorem 14.7). MinUnsafeAdd is NP-hard in general; the single-edge case is polynomial (O⁡(n3​k2)O(n^{3}k^{2})); the greedy defence achieves a (1−1/e)(1-1/e) approximation to optimal by submodularity of the robustness function in the hyperedge set.

1.4 Related Work

Directed hypergraphs.

The foundations used here—reachability, closure, and B-graphs—were laid by Gallo et al. (1993) and surveyed by Ausiello and Laura (2017). Our closure operator is a restriction of their reachability notion to the AND-semantics case; the connection to Horn clause inference is classical (van Emden and Kowalski, 1976) and forms the logical foundation for Theorem 6.3.

Petri nets.

Petri nets (Petri, 1962; Murata, 1989) are a closely related formalism. Our framework differs in two key respects: capabilities are treated as persistent (once derived, always available) rather than consumed by firing, and the focus is on goal discovery and safety certification rather than concurrency analysis.

HTN and AND/OR planning.

Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning (Erol et al., 1994) and AND/OR planning graphs (Bonet and Geffner, 2001) both encode conjunctive preconditions. The key distinction is that these formalisms are designed for heuristic search over task-decomposition trees, not for formal safety certification. In particular, neither provides (i) a closure-based characterisation that is both sound and complete without search, (ii) the non-compositionality theorem, nor (iii) a polynomial-time certifiable audit surface.

Submodular optimisation.

Submodular optimisation (Nemhauser et al., 1978; Fujishige, 2005) provides the theoretical basis for our greedy acquisition guarantee. The connection between closure systems and submodularity via the polymatroid rank theorem (Theorem 8.5) is standard; our contribution is applying this to the capability-acquisition setting and connecting it to the safety boundary.

The adjacent possible.

The concept of the adjacent possible (Kauffman, 2000)—the set of states one step beyond the current state of a complex system—anticipates our near-miss frontier informally. We provide a formal algebraic characterisation (Proposition 8.2) and prove that it coincides exactly with the unit-distance boundary under the acquisition distance metric.

AI safety and compositionality.

Concerns about emergent dangerous capabilities in composed AI systems have been raised informally in the AI safety literature (Russell and Norvig, 2021; Yao et al., 2023). To our knowledge, Theorem 9.2 is the first formal proof of non-compositionality in the capability-composition setting.

Compositional verification and assume-guarantee reasoning.

The formal methods community has studied safety in composed systems for decades under the heading of compositional verification (Clarke et al., 1999; Pnueli, 1977). The dominant paradigm is assume-guarantee reasoning (Jones, 1983): a component CiC_{i} is verified under an assumption AiA_{i} about its environment. Contract-based design (Benveniste et al., 2018; Sangiovanni-Vincentelli et al., 2012) formalises this idea. Our setting is complementary but structurally distinct in three respects. First, assume-guarantee reasoning verifies that a fixed composition satisfies a pre-specified global property; we instead characterise the set of all properties a dynamically growing capability set can ever reach. Second, the non-compositionality result addresses a failure mode that assume-guarantee reasoning is specifically designed to prevent—yet it cannot prevent it here, because the failure arises not from a component violating its guarantee but from two individually correct components producing a conjunctive emergent capability when combined. Third, the complexity of our safety audit (Theorem 9.5: coNP-complete) aligns with known lower bounds for contract composition and compatibility checking (de Alfaro and Henzinger, 2001; Bauer et al., 2012).

Interface automata (de Alfaro and Henzinger, 2001) and modal interface theories (Raclet et al., 2011) provide the closest formal analogy. The key difference is that these theories treat components as reactive systems with input/output alphabets, whereas our capability nodes are propositional facts with no internal dynamics. This restriction—capabilities as persistent atomic facts rather than stateful processes—is precisely what enables the Horn clause completeness result (Theorem 6.3) and reduces planning from PSPACE to polynomial time.

2 Capability-Based System Modelling

2.1 Capabilities

A capability represents a functional ability of a system to perform a computational or informational transformation—for example, speech recognition, intent extraction, database query execution, reasoning over knowledge graphs, or text generation. Capabilities may correspond to AI models, software services, tools, API calls, or human-assisted processes.

2.2 Capability Graphs and Their Limitation

Definition 2.1 (Capability Graph).

A capability graph is a directed graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) where VV is a finite set of capability nodes and E⊆V×VE\subseteq V\times V is a set of directed edges. The edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E encodes: possession of uu alone is sufficient to make vv available.

The capability closure of a set A⊆VA\subseteq V in a graph is standard graph reachability: clG(A)={v∈V:∃u∈A,u→∗v}∪A.\mathrm{cl}_{G}(A)=\{v\in V:\exists u\in A,\,u\to^{*}v\}\cup A.

Fundamental limitation.

A capability graph can only encode sufficient singleton preconditions. It cannot express:

  • •

    Conjunction: vv requires both u1u_{1} and u2u_{2}.

  • •

    Joint emergence: u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} together produce vv, but neither alone does.

  • •

    Multi-target yield: firing uu simultaneously produces v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} as an inseparable unit.

Any attempt to encode conjunction in a plain graph requires an artificial intermediate node—say, a node called u1∧u2u_{1}\wedge u_{2}—which pollutes VV with logical artefacts rather than genuine capabilities. This is not merely an aesthetic concern: as Theorem 9.2 shows, it is the source of a provable safety failure.

3 Directed Hypergraphs

Definition 3.1 (Directed Hypergraph).

A directed hypergraph is a pair H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) where VV is a finite set of vertices and ℱ\mathcal{F} is a set of hyperarcs, each of the form e=(S,T)e=(S,T) with S,T⊆VS,T\subseteq V and S∩T=∅S\cap T=\emptyset. The set SS is the tail (preconditions) and TT is the head (effects). The hyperarc fires when all elements of SS are simultaneously present, producing all elements of TT simultaneously. Directed graphs are the special case where |S|=|T|=1|S|=|T|=1 for every hyperarc.

Definition 3.2 (Capability Hypergraph).

A capability hypergraph is a directed hypergraph H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) where vertices represent capabilities and each hyperarc (S,T)∈ℱ(S,T)\in\mathcal{F} represents a composition rule: the capabilities in SS jointly enable those in TT.

5 Embedding Capability Graphs into Hypergraphs

Lemma 5.1 (Graph Embedding, cf. Gallo et al. 1993).

Every capability graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) can be faithfully represented as a directed hypergraph H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) in which every hyperedge has both a singleton tail and a singleton head: |S|=|T|=1|S|=|T|=1 for all (S,T)∈ℱ(S,T)\in\mathcal{F}. The representation preserves the reachability relation exactly: clG​(A)=clH​(A)\mathrm{cl}_{G}(A)=\mathrm{cl}_{H}(A) for every A⊆VA\subseteq V.

Proof.

Construct ℱ={({u},{v}):(u,v)∈E}\mathcal{F}=\{(\{u\},\{v\}):(u,v)\in E\}.

(⊆)(\subseteq) By induction on the length of the shortest path in GG from AA to vv: base case v∈Av\in A follows from extensivity; inductive step uses the singleton hyperedge ({wn−1},{wn})∈ℱ(\{w_{n-1}\},\{w_{n}\})\in\mathcal{F}.

(⊇)(\supseteq) Every hyperedge in ℱ\mathcal{F} has the form ({u},{v})(\{u\},\{v\}) with (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E, giving exactly graph reachability. Hence clG​(A)\mathrm{cl}_{G}(A) satisfies both closure axioms for HH, so clH​(A)⊆clG​(A)\mathrm{cl}_{H}(A)\subseteq\mathrm{cl}_{G}(A) by minimality. ∎

Corollary 5.2 (Strict Generalisation).

The class of directed hypergraphs with singleton head sets strictly contains the class of capability graphs.

Proof.

Let V={u1,u2,v}V=\{u_{1},u_{2},v\} and H=(V,{({u1,u2},{v})})H=(V,\{(\{u_{1},u_{2}\},\{v\})\}). Then clH​({u1})={u1}\mathrm{cl}_{H}(\{u_{1}\})=\{u_{1}\}, clH​({u2})={u2}\mathrm{cl}_{H}(\{u_{2}\})=\{u_{2}\}, but clH​({u1,u2})={u1,u2,v}\mathrm{cl}_{H}(\{u_{1},u_{2}\})=\{u_{1},u_{2},v\}. Suppose for contradiction a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) satisfies clG​(A)=clH​(A)\mathrm{cl}_{G}(A)=\mathrm{cl}_{H}(A) for all AA. From the first two closures, neither u1u_{1} nor u2u_{2} can reach vv in GG. But the third requires a path from {u1,u2}\{u_{1},u_{2}\} to vv in GG. Contradiction. ∎

6 Capability Closure and Planning

6.1 The Closure Operator

Definition 6.1 (Closure Operator).

Let H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) be a capability hypergraph and A⊆VA\subseteq V. The closure cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}(A) is the smallest set C⊆VC\subseteq V satisfying:

  1. 1.

    A⊆CA\subseteq C (extensivity)

  2. 2.

    ∀(S,T)∈ℱ:S⊆C⇒T⊆C\forall(S,T)\in\mathcal{F}:S\subseteq C\Rightarrow T\subseteq C (closed under firing)

Computed by the fixed-point iteration C0=AC_{0}=A, Ci+1=Ci∪{T∣(S,T)∈ℱ,S⊆Ci}C_{i+1}=C_{i}\cup\{T\mid(S,T)\in\mathcal{F},\,S\subseteq C_{i}\}, terminating in at most |V||V| steps.

The operator satisfies extensivity (A⊆cl⁡(A)A\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A)), monotonicity (A⊆B⇒cl⁡(A)⊆cl⁡(B)A\subseteq B\Rightarrow\mathrm{cl}(A)\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(B)), and idempotence (cl⁡(cl⁡(A))=cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{cl}(A))=\mathrm{cl}(A)), making (V,cl)(V,\mathrm{cl}) a closure system (Moore family) (Ganter and Wille, 1999).

6.2 Planning as Closure

Definition 6.2 (Plan).

A plan from AA in H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) is a finite sequence of hyperedges π=(e1,…,en)\pi=(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}) with ei=(Si,Ti)∈ℱe_{i}=(S_{i},T_{i})\in\mathcal{F}, and sets A=D0⊆D1⊆⋯⊆Dn⊆VA=D_{0}\subseteq D_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq D_{n}\subseteq V, satisfying: (1) Si⊆Di−1S_{i}\subseteq D_{i-1} (applicability); (2) Di=Di−1∪TiD_{i}=D_{i-1}\cup T_{i} (effect). A plan π\pi achieves goal G⊆VG\subseteq V if G⊆DnG\subseteq D_{n}.

Theorem 6.3 (Planning as Closure).

Let H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) be a capability hypergraph, A⊆VA\subseteq V an initial capability set, and G⊆VG\subseteq V a goal set. A plan from AA achieving GG exists if and only if G⊆cl⁡(A)G\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A).

Proof.

(⇒)(\Rightarrow) By induction on plan length nn, we show Dn⊆cl⁡(A)D_{n}\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A). Base case: D0=A⊆cl⁡(A)D_{0}=A\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A). Inductive step: if Di−1⊆cl⁡(A)D_{i-1}\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A) then Si⊆cl⁡(A)S_{i}\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A), so Ti⊆cl⁡(A)T_{i}\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A), giving Di⊆cl⁡(A)D_{i}\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A).

(⇐)(\Leftarrow) Run the fixed-point iteration. Enumerate hyperedges in non-decreasing order of first-applicable step; set D0=AD_{0}=A and Dj=Dj−1∪TjD_{j}=D_{j-1}\cup T_{j}. Applicability and achievement hold by construction. ∎

Remark 6.4 (Isomorphism with Horn clause forward chaining).

Theorem 6.3 is the capability-hypergraph instance of the completeness theorem for definite Horn clause forward chaining (van Emden and Kowalski, 1976). Each capability v∈Vv\in V corresponds to a propositional atom; each hyperarc (S,T)(S,T) with S={s1,…,sk}S=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}\} corresponds to the Horn clause s1∧⋯∧sk→ts_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge s_{k}\to t for each t∈Tt\in T. The closure cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}(A) equals the minimal Herbrand model of A∪ℱA\cup\mathcal{F}, which by the van Emden–Kowalski theorem equals the least fixed point of the immediate consequence operator TPT_{P}. The worklist algorithm (Algorithm 1) is an optimised implementation of the TP↑ωT_{P}\uparrow\omega sequence: counter arrays reduce the O⁡(n⋅m⋅k)O(n\cdot m\cdot k) naive cost to O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk).

6.3 Properties of the Closure Operator

Planning question Formal reduction
Is goal GG achievable? G⊆cl⁡(A)G\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A)?
What is the full reach of AA? Compute cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}(A)
What is the capability gap? G∖cl⁡(A)G\setminus\mathrm{cl}(A)
Which single addition unlocks the most? arg⁡maxv∈V∖A​|cl⁡(A∪{v})|\arg\max_{v\in V\setminus A}|\mathrm{cl}(A\cup\{v\})|

7 Capability Closure Algorithm

Each capability enters the worklist at most once (O⁡(n)O(n) total); each hyperedge counter is decremented at most kk times (O⁡(m​k)O(mk) total). Overall complexity: O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk), linear in hypergraph size.

8 Goal Discovery via Hypergraph Closure

Traditional AI systems are given goals externally. The hypergraph closure framework enables an agent to discover goals it did not know were possible by observing the topology of its own capability space: goal discovery is an intrinsic consequence of closure computation, not a separate process.

8.1 Formal Definitions

Fix H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) and A⊆VA\subseteq V. Let C=cl⁡(A)C=\mathrm{cl}(A). Let cl1​(A)\mathrm{cl}_{1}(A) denote the closure under the sub-hypergraph ℱ1={(S,T)∈ℱ:|S|=1}\mathcal{F}_{1}=\{(S,T)\in\mathcal{F}:|S|=1\} of singleton-tail hyperedges only; by definition cl1​(A)⊆cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}_{1}(A)\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A).

Definition 8.1 (Goal Discovery Structures).
  1. (a)

    Emergent capabilities: Emg⁡(A)={v∈C∖A:v∉cl1​(A)}\mathrm{Emg}(A)=\{v\in C\setminus A:v\notin\mathrm{cl}_{1}(A)\}.

  2. (b)

    Closure boundary: ∂(A)={(S,T)∈ℱ:S⊈C,|S∖C|=1}\partial(A)=\{(S,T)\in\mathcal{F}:S\not\subseteq C,\ |S\setminus C|=1\}.

  3. (c)

    Near-miss frontier: NMF⁡(A)={μ⁡(e):e∈∂(A)}\mathrm{NMF}(A)=\{\mu(e):e\in\partial(A)\} where μ⁡(e)=S∖C\mu(e)=S\setminus C.

  4. (d)

    Marginal closure gain: γ⁡(v,A)=|cl⁡(A∪{v})|−|cl⁡(A)|\gamma(v,A)=|\mathrm{cl}(A\cup\{v\})|-|\mathrm{cl}(A)| for v∈V∖Cv\in V\setminus C.

  5. (e)

    Acquisition distance: δ(g,A)=min{|S|:S⊆V∖C,g∈cl(A∪S)}\delta(g,A)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq V\setminus C,\ g\in\mathrm{cl}(A\cup S)\}, or ∞\infty if no such SS exists.

8.3 Goal Discovery Proposition

Proposition 8.2 (Goal Discovery Structure).

Fix H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}), A⊆VA\subseteq V, C=cl⁡(A)C=\mathrm{cl}(A).

  1. 1.

    Emergent capability characterisation. Emg⁡(A)≠∅\mathrm{Emg}(A)\neq\emptyset iff there exists (S,T)∈ℱ(S,T)\in\mathcal{F} with |S|≥2|S|\geq 2, S⊆CS\subseteq C, and T⊈cl1​(A)T\not\subseteq\mathrm{cl}_{1}(A).

    Boundary dynamics. Let v∗∈NMF⁡(A)v^{*}\in\mathrm{NMF}(A) and A′=A∪{v∗}A^{\prime}=A\cup\{v^{*}\}. Then every e∈∂(A)e\in\partial(A) with μ⁡(e)={v∗}\mu(e)=\{v^{*}\} leaves the boundary, and NMF⁡(A′)≠NMF⁡(A)\mathrm{NMF}(A^{\prime})\neq\mathrm{NMF}(A) whenever cl⁡(A′)⊋C\mathrm{cl}(A^{\prime})\supsetneq C.

  3. 3.

    NMF biconditional. For any g∈Vg\in V and A⊆VA\subseteq V: δ⁡(g,A)=0\delta(g,A)=0 iff g∈Cg\in C; and NMF⁡(A)={v∈V∖C:cl⁡(A∪{v})⊋C}\mathrm{NMF}(A)=\{v\in V\setminus C:\mathrm{cl}(A\cup\{v\})\supsetneq C\}.

    Robustness monotonicity. Define the robustness ρ⁡(v,A)\rho(v,A) as the number of minimal acquisition sets S⊆V∖CS\subseteq V\setminus C such that v∈cl⁡(A∪S)v\in\mathrm{cl}(A\cup S). For all v∈Vv\in V and u∈V∖Cu\in V\setminus C: ρ⁡(v,A∪{u})≥ρ⁡(v,A)\rho(v,A\cup\{u\})\geq\rho(v,A).

8.4 Computational Hardness of Emergent Capability Detection

Theorem 8.3 (P-Completeness of Emergent Detection).

The problem EmergentDetect: given H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) and A⊆VA\subseteq V, decide whether Emg⁡(A)≠∅\mathrm{Emg}(A)\neq\emptyset, is P-complete under log-space reductions.

Proof.

Membership in P. Algorithm 2 runs in time O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk).

P-hardness. We reduce from the monotone Circuit Value Problem (CVP), which is P-complete under log-space reductions (Ladner, 1975; Goldschlager, 1977). Given a monotone Boolean circuit CC with inputs x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}, designated output gate g∗g^{*}, and assignment a∈{0,1}na\in\{0,1\}^{n}, construct (H,A′)(H,A^{\prime}) as follows. For each gate gig_{i} in CC, create vertex vi∈Vv_{i}\in V. Set A′={vi:ai=1}∪{v⊤}A^{\prime}=\{v_{i}:a_{i}=1\}\cup\{v_{\top}\} where v⊤v_{\top} is a fresh vertex. For each AND-gate gig_{i} with inputs gj,gkg_{j},g_{k}: add hyperedge ({vj,vk},{vi})(\{v_{j},v_{k}\},\{v_{i}\}). For each OR-gate gig_{i} with inputs gj,gkg_{j},g_{k}: add singleton-tail hyperedges ({vj},{vi})(\{v_{j}\},\{v_{i}\}) and ({vk},{vi})(\{v_{k}\},\{v_{i}\}). Add a fresh vertex vemgv_{\mathrm{emg}} and the hyperedge ({vg∗},{vemg})(\{v_{g^{*}}\},\{v_{\mathrm{emg}}\}). If g∗g^{*} is an OR-gate, prepend a synthetic AND-gate g∗⁣∗g^{**} with inputs g∗g^{*} and v⊤v_{\top}. By induction on circuit depth, vg∗∈cl⁡(A′)v_{g^{*}}\in\mathrm{cl}(A^{\prime}) iff C⁡(a)=1C(a)=1. The synthetic AND-gate ensures vg∗∉cl1​(A′)v_{g^{*}}\notin\mathrm{cl}_{1}(A^{\prime}) when C⁡(a)=1C(a)=1. Therefore vemg∈Emg⁡(A′)v_{\mathrm{emg}}\in\mathrm{Emg}(A^{\prime}) iff C⁡(a)=1C(a)=1. ∎

Corollary 8.4.

EmergentDetect is P-complete, placing it outside NC under standard complexity assumptions (NC≠P\mathrm{NC}\neq\mathrm{P}).

8.5 Submodularity and Greedy Acquisition

Theorem 8.5 (Submodularity of Closure Gain).

Define f:2V∖cl⁡(A)→ℕf:2^{V\setminus\mathrm{cl}(A)}\to\mathbb{N} by f⁡(B)=|cl⁡(A∪B)|−|cl⁡(A)|f(B)=|\mathrm{cl}(A\cup B)|-|\mathrm{cl}(A)|. Then ff is normalised (f⁡(∅)=0f(\emptyset)=0), monotone, and submodular: for all B⊆C′⊆V∖cl⁡(A)B\subseteq C^{\prime}\subseteq V\setminus\mathrm{cl}(A) and v∈(V∖cl⁡(A))∖C′v\in(V\setminus\mathrm{cl}(A))\setminus C^{\prime},

f⁡(B∪{v})−f⁡(B)≥f⁡(C′∪{v})−f⁡(C′).f(B\cup\{v\})-f(B)\geq f(C^{\prime}\cup\{v\})-f(C^{\prime}).
Proof.

The closure operator satisfies extensivity, monotonicity, and idempotence, making (V,cl)(V,\mathrm{cl}) a finite closure system. By Theorem 3.3 of Fujishige (2005), the rank function g⁡(X)=|cl⁡(X)|g(X)=|\mathrm{cl}(X)| of any finite closure system satisfies the diminishing returns property: for all X⊆Y⊆VX\subseteq Y\subseteq V and v∈V∖Yv\in V\setminus Y, g⁡(X∪{v})−g⁡(X)≥g⁡(Y∪{v})−g⁡(Y).g(X\cup\{v\})-g(X)\geq g(Y\cup\{v\})-g(Y). Set X=A∪BX=A\cup B and Y=A∪C′Y=A\cup C^{\prime}. Since B⊆C′B\subseteq C^{\prime} we have X⊆YX\subseteq Y, and since v∈(V∖cl⁡(A))∖C′v\in(V\setminus\mathrm{cl}(A))\setminus C^{\prime} we have v∉Yv\notin Y. Substituting gives the required inequality. ∎

Corollary 8.6 (Greedy Approximation Guarantee).

Let k≥1k\geq 1, let B∗=arg⁡max|B|≤k⁡f⁡(B)B^{*}=\arg\max_{|B|\leq k}f(B), and let v∗=arg⁡maxv∈V∖C⁡γ⁡(v,A)v^{*}=\arg\max_{v\in V\setminus C}\gamma(v,A) (the greedy step). Then f⁡(Bgreedy)≥(1−1/e)⋅f⁡(B∗).f(B_{\mathrm{greedy}})\geq(1-1/e)\cdot f(B^{*}).

Proof.

Since f⁡(∅)=0f(\emptyset)=0, ff is monotone, and ff is submodular (Theorem 8.5), the three preconditions of Nemhauser et al. (1978) are satisfied and their theorem applies directly. ∎

9 Safety and Containment

Definition 9.1 (Forbidden Set and Safe Region).

Let F⊆VF\subseteq V be a forbidden set. A capability set A⊆VA\subseteq V is FF-contained if cl⁡(A)∩F=∅\mathrm{cl}(A)\cap F=\emptyset. The safe region is ℛ⁡(F)={A⊆V:cl⁡(A)∩F=∅}\mathcal{R}(F)=\{A\subseteq V:\mathrm{cl}(A)\cap F=\emptyset\}.

Theorem 9.2 (Non-Compositionality of Safety).

Let F⊆VF\subseteq V be a forbidden set. The safe region ℛ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}(F) is not closed under union in general: there exist A,B∈ℛ⁡(F)A,B\in\mathcal{R}(F) such that A∪B∉ℛ⁡(F)A\cup B\notin\mathcal{R}(F). Equivalently: two agents each individually incapable of reaching any forbidden capability may, when combined, collectively reach a forbidden goal.

This is the first formal proof of this result in the capability-composition setting.

Proof.

Minimal counterexample. Let V={u1,u2,f}V=\{u_{1},u_{2},f\}, F={f}F=\{f\}, and ℱ={({u1,u2},{f})}\mathcal{F}=\{(\{u_{1},u_{2}\},\{f\})\}. Set A={u1}A=\{u_{1}\} and B={u2}B=\{u_{2}\}.

A∈ℛ⁡(F)A\in\mathcal{R}(F): the only hyperedge requires u2u_{2}, which is absent from AA, so cl⁡({u1})={u1}\mathrm{cl}(\{u_{1}\})=\{u_{1}\}.

B∈ℛ⁡(F)B\in\mathcal{R}(F): by the same argument, cl⁡({u2})={u2}\mathrm{cl}(\{u_{2}\})=\{u_{2}\}.

A∪B∉ℛ⁡(F)A\cup B\notin\mathcal{R}(F): {u1,u2}\{u_{1},u_{2}\} satisfies the hyperedge’s precondition, so cl⁡({u1,u2})={u1,u2,f}\mathrm{cl}(\{u_{1},u_{2}\})=\{u_{1},u_{2},f\} and cl⁡(A∪B)∩{f}={f}≠∅\mathrm{cl}(A\cup B)\cap\{f\}=\{f\}\neq\emptyset.

Minimality. With |V|<3|V|<3 there is no room for two safe sets whose union reaches a distinct forbidden vertex. Without a multi-input hyperedge (i.e. in any capability graph), cl⁡(A∪B)=cl⁡(A)∪cl⁡(B)\mathrm{cl}(A\cup B)=\mathrm{cl}(A)\cup\mathrm{cl}(B) when cl⁡(A)∩cl⁡(B)=∅\mathrm{cl}(A)\cap\mathrm{cl}(B)=\emptyset, so the failure cannot arise. The AND-semantics of a conjunctive hyperedge is the irreducible source of non-compositionality. ∎

Remark 9.3.

In a capability graph (all tails singleton), monotonicity gives cl⁡(A∪B)⊇cl⁡(A)∪cl⁡(B)\mathrm{cl}(A\cup B)\supseteq\mathrm{cl}(A)\cup\mathrm{cl}(B) always, so the failure mode of Theorem 9.2 cannot arise. Two agents holding {u1}\{u_{1}\} and {u2}\{u_{2}\} are each graph-safe regardless of what cl⁡({u1})\mathrm{cl}(\{u_{1}\}) and cl⁡({u2})\mathrm{cl}(\{u_{2}\}) share, because no pairwise graph edge can encode the joint precondition {u1,u2}\{u_{1},u_{2}\}.

Theorem 9.4 (Lattice Structure of the Safe Region).

Let F⊆VF\subseteq V be a forbidden set. The safe region ℛ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}(F) is a lower set (downward-closed) in (2V,⊆)(2^{V},\subseteq): if A∈ℛ⁡(F)A\in\mathcal{R}(F) and B⊆AB\subseteq A, then B∈ℛ⁡(F)B\in\mathcal{R}(F). Consequently:

  1. 1.

    Every subset of a safe set is safe.

  2. 2.

    ℛ⁡(F)¯=2V∖ℛ⁡(F)\overline{\mathcal{R}(F)}=2^{V}\setminus\mathcal{R}(F) is an upper set.

  3. 3.

    The boundary of the safe region is exactly the finite antichain of minimal unsafe sets: ℬ(F)={A⊆V:A∉ℛ(F),∀a∈A,A∖{a}∈ℛ(F)}\mathcal{B}(F)=\{A\subseteq V:A\notin\mathcal{R}(F),\ \forall a\in A,\ A\setminus\{a\}\in\mathcal{R}(F)\}.

  4. 4.

    ℛ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}(F) is closed under pairwise intersection (a Moore family under ∩\cap) but not under union (Theorem 9.2).

Proof.

(1) If cl⁡(A)∩F=∅\mathrm{cl}(A)\cap F=\emptyset and B⊆AB\subseteq A, then cl⁡(B)⊆cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}(B)\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A) by monotonicity. (2) If cl⁡(A)∩F≠∅\mathrm{cl}(A)\cap F\neq\emptyset and B⊇AB\supseteq A, then cl⁡(B)⊇cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}(B)\supseteq\mathrm{cl}(A). (3) ℬ⁡(F)\mathcal{B}(F) is the antichain of minimal elements of ℛ⁡(F)¯\overline{\mathcal{R}(F)}, finite and unique by Dickson’s lemma. (4) If A,B∈ℛ⁡(F)A,B\in\mathcal{R}(F) then A∩B⊆AA\cap B\subseteq A, so (1) gives A∩B∈ℛ⁡(F)A\cap B\in\mathcal{R}(F). ∎

Theorem 9.5 (Hardness of Computing the Minimal Unsafe Antichain).

The problem MinUnsafeAnt: given H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}), forbidden set FF, and B⊆VB\subseteq V, decide whether B∈ℬ⁡(F)B\in\mathcal{B}(F), is coNP-complete.

Proof.

Membership in coNP. The complement B∉ℬ⁡(F)B\notin\mathcal{B}(F) has two polynomial-time-verifiable certificates: (a) cl⁡(B)∩F=∅\mathrm{cl}(B)\cap F=\emptyset, or (b) ∃b∈B\exists b\in B with cl⁡(B∖{b})∩F≠∅\mathrm{cl}(B\setminus\{b\})\cap F\neq\emptyset.

coNP-hardness. We reduce from MinTransversal: given a hypergraph H=(U,ℰ)H=(U,\mathcal{E}) and T⊆UT\subseteq U, decide whether TT is a minimal transversal of HH. This problem is coNP-complete (Eiter and Gottlob, 1995). Given (H,T)(H,T) with H=(U,ℰ)H=(U,\mathcal{E}), build (H′,F′,B′)(H^{\prime},F^{\prime},B^{\prime}) as follows. Let V′=U∪{fE:E∈ℰ}∪{f∗}V^{\prime}=U\cup\{f_{E}:E\in\mathcal{E}\}\cup\{f^{*}\}. For each E={u1,…,uℓ}∈ℰE=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{\ell}\}\in\mathcal{E}, add singleton hyperedges {({ui},{fE}):ui∈E}\{(\{u_{i}\},\{f_{E}\}):u_{i}\in E\}. Add the hyperedge ({fE:E∈ℰ},{f∗})(\{f_{E}:E\in\mathcal{E}\},\{f^{*}\}). Set F′={f∗}F^{\prime}=\{f^{*}\} and B′=TB^{\prime}=T. Then B′∈ℬ⁡(F′)B^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}(F^{\prime}) iff TT is a minimal transversal. ∎

Definition 9.6 (Safe Acquisition Path).

A safe acquisition path to goal gg from AA is a sequence A=A0⊊A1⊊⋯⊊AmA=A_{0}\subsetneq A_{1}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq A_{m} with Ai+1=Ai∪{vi}A_{i+1}=A_{i}\cup\{v_{i}\}, vi∈V∖cl⁡(Ai)v_{i}\in V\setminus\mathrm{cl}(A_{i}), Ai∈ℛ⁡(F)A_{i}\in\mathcal{R}(F) for all ii, and g∈cl⁡(Am)g\in\mathrm{cl}(A_{m}). The safe acquisition distance δF​(g,A)\delta_{F}(g,A) is the minimum mm, or ∞\infty.

Theorem 9.7 (Safe Acquisition Path Decidability).

Given F⊆VF\subseteq V, A∈ℛ⁡(F)A\in\mathcal{R}(F), and g∈V∖Fg\in V\setminus F, deciding whether a safe acquisition path to gg exists is decidable by BFS over the safe acquisition graph. Goals g∈V∖Fg\in V\setminus F are classified into exactly three types: (1) already reachable: g∈cl⁡(A)g\in\mathrm{cl}(A); (2) safely acquirable; (3) structurally unsafe: every path to gg passes through FF.

10 The Safe Audit Surface Theorem

Theorem 10.1 (Safe Audit Surface).

Let H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) be a capability hypergraph, A⊆VA\subseteq V a deployment configuration, and F⊆VF\subseteq V a forbidden set with A∈ℛ⁡(F)A\in\mathcal{R}(F). Define the safe goal discovery map:

GF(A)=(Emg(A)∖F,NMFF(A),argtop-kv∈V∖(cl⁡(A)∪F)γF(v,A)),G_{F}(A)=\left(\mathrm{Emg}(A)\setminus F,\quad\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A),\quad\mathrm{arg\,top\text{-}k}_{v\in V\setminus(\mathrm{cl}(A)\cup F)}\gamma_{F}(v,A)\right),

where

NMFF(A)={μ(e):e∈∂(A),μ(e)∉F,cl(A∪μ(e))∩F=∅},\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A)=\{\mu(e):e\in\partial(A),\ \mu(e)\notin F,\ \mathrm{cl}(A\cup\mu(e))\cap F=\emptyset\},
γF​(v,A)=|cl⁡(A∪{v})∖(cl⁡(A)∪F)|.\gamma_{F}(v,A)=|\mathrm{cl}(A\cup\{v\})\setminus(\mathrm{cl}(A)\cup F)|.

Then GF​(A)G_{F}(A) has the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Completeness. Every capability that is safely acquirable from AA appears in some component of GF​(A)G_{F}(A) or is reachable from a goal in GF​(A)G_{F}(A).

  2. 2.

    Soundness. Every goal in Emg⁡(A)∖F\mathrm{Emg}(A)\setminus F is reachable from AA without leaving ℛ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}(F). Every goal in NMFF​(A)\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A) is one acquisition step away from expanding the closure while remaining safe.

  3. 3.

    Efficient computability. GF​(A)G_{F}(A) is computable in time O⁡(|V|⋅(n+m​k))O(|V|\cdot(n+mk))—polynomial in the size of the hypergraph.

  4. 4.

    Certifiability. Each v∈Emg⁡(A)∖Fv\in\mathrm{Emg}(A)\setminus F comes with a derivation certificate. Each v∈NMFF​(A)v\in\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A) comes with the boundary hyperedge it would unlock. Each structurally unsafe goal comes with a proof that every acquisition path passes through FF.

Proof.

(1) Completeness. Let vv be any safely acquirable capability; by Theorem 9.7 there is a safe acquisition path A=A0⊊⋯⊊AmA=A_{0}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq A_{m} with v∈cl⁡(Am)v\in\mathrm{cl}(A_{m}) and every Ai∈ℛ⁡(F)A_{i}\in\mathcal{R}(F). If m=0m=0 then v∈cl⁡(A)v\in\mathrm{cl}(A). If m=1m=1 then v0∈NMFF​(A)v_{0}\in\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A) or vv is in the top-kk structural goals. If m≥2m\geq 2, then vv is reachable from a goal in NMFF​(A)\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A) by iterating the boundary argument.

(2) Soundness. Let v∈Emg⁡(A)∖Fv\in\mathrm{Emg}(A)\setminus F; by definition v∈cl⁡(A)v\in\mathrm{cl}(A), so vv is reachable from AA by Theorem 6.3 without any acquisition. Let v∈NMFF​(A)v\in\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A); by definition μ⁡(e)∉F\mu(e)\notin F and cl⁡(A∪μ⁡(e))∩F=∅\mathrm{cl}(A\cup\mu(e))\cap F=\emptyset, so acquiring μ⁡(e)\mu(e) keeps the agent in ℛ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}(F).

(3) Efficient computability. One full closure call costs O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk). The singleton-closure sub-call costs O⁡(n+m)O(n+m). The boundary scan costs O⁡(m​k)O(mk). The marginal gain loop runs |V∖cl⁡(A)|≤|V||V\setminus\mathrm{cl}(A)|\leq|V| closure calls: O⁡(|V|⋅(n+m​k))O(|V|\cdot(n+mk)) total.

(4) Certifiability. The worklist records, for each newly reached vertex vv, the firing sequence that produced it. For v∈NMFF​(A)v\in\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A), the boundary scan records the boundary hyperedge e∈∂(A)e\in\partial(A) with μ⁡(e)=v\mu(e)=v. For structurally unsafe vv: BFS over 𝒜⁡(F,A)\mathcal{A}(F,A) exhausts all safe acquisition paths and finds none reaching vv. ∎

11 Extensions: Multi-Agent Composition and Dynamic Hypergraphs

11.1 Multi-Agent Coalition Safety

Definition 11.1 (Coalition).

A coalition is a finite collection of agents 𝒜={a1,…,an}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\}, each with an associated capability set Ai⊆VA_{i}\subseteq V. The joint capability set of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is ⋃i=1nAi\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}.

Theorem 11.2 (Coalition Safety Criterion).

Let H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) be a capability hypergraph, F⊆VF\subseteq V a forbidden set, and 𝒜={a1,…,an}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\} a coalition with individual capability sets A1,…,An∈ℛ⁡(F)A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\in\mathcal{R}(F). The coalition is unsafe if and only if there exists a minimal unsafe set B∈ℬ⁡(F)B\in\mathcal{B}(F) such that B⊆⋃i=1nAiB\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}.

Proof.

(⇒)(\Rightarrow) Suppose ⋃iAi∉ℛ⁡(F)\bigcup_{i}A_{i}\notin\mathcal{R}(F). By the upper-set property (Theorem 9.4(2)), ⋃iAi\bigcup_{i}A_{i} is unsafe. The unsafe region ℛ⁡(F)¯\overline{\mathcal{R}(F)} is an upper set with minimal elements ℬ⁡(F)\mathcal{B}(F), so there exists B∈ℬ⁡(F)B\in\mathcal{B}(F) with B⊆⋃iAiB\subseteq\bigcup_{i}A_{i}.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow) Suppose B⊆⋃iAiB\subseteq\bigcup_{i}A_{i} for some B∈ℬ⁡(F)B\in\mathcal{B}(F). Since B∉ℛ⁡(F)B\notin\mathcal{R}(F), we have cl⁡(B)∩F≠∅\mathrm{cl}(B)\cap F\neq\emptyset. By monotonicity of cl\mathrm{cl}, cl⁡(⋃iAi)⊇cl⁡(B)\mathrm{cl}(\bigcup_{i}A_{i})\supseteq\mathrm{cl}(B), so cl⁡(⋃iAi)∩F≠∅\mathrm{cl}(\bigcup_{i}A_{i})\cap F\neq\emptyset. ∎

Remark 11.3.

Theorem 11.2 reduces coalition safety checking to a single set-cover query against the precomputed antichain ℬ⁡(F)\mathcal{B}(F). Once ℬ⁡(F)\mathcal{B}(F) is computed offline, every subsequent coalition query takes time O⁡(|ℬ⁡(F)|⋅∑i|Ai|)O(|\mathcal{B}(F)|\cdot\sum_{i}|A_{i}|)—linear in the total capability count.

Corollary 11.4 (Maximal Safe Coalition).

A coalition 𝒜\mathcal{A} is maximally safe if it is FF-contained and no agent can be added without violating safety. The set of maximally safe coalitions corresponds exactly to the antichain of maximal elements of ℛ⁡(F)\mathcal{R}(F) under set inclusion of joint capability sets.

11.2 Dynamic Capability Hypergraphs

Definition 11.5 (Dynamic Hypergraph).

A dynamic capability hypergraph is a finite sequence of hypergraphs H0,H1,…H_{0},H_{1},\ldots where Ht=(V,ℱt)H_{t}=(V,\mathcal{F}_{t}) is obtained from Ht−1H_{t-1} by either a hyperedge insertion (ℱt=ℱt−1∪{e}\mathcal{F}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\cup\{e\}) or deletion (ℱt=ℱt−1∖{e}\mathcal{F}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\setminus\{e\}).

Theorem 11.6 (Incremental Closure Maintenance).

Let H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}), A⊆VA\subseteq V, and C=clH​(A)C=\mathrm{cl}_{H}(A).

  1. 1.

    Insertion. Let e=(S,T)e=(S,T) be a new hyperedge and H′=(V,ℱ∪{e})H^{\prime}=(V,\mathcal{F}\cup\{e\}). Then clH′​(A)=clH​(A∪T′)\mathrm{cl}_{H^{\prime}}(A)=\mathrm{cl}_{H}(A\cup T^{\prime}) where T′=TT^{\prime}=T if S⊆CS\subseteq C, else T′=∅T^{\prime}=\emptyset. The update costs O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk) in the worst case and O⁡(|S|)O(|S|) when S⊈CS\not\subseteq C.

  2. 2.

    Deletion. Let e=(S,T)e=(S,T) be a removed hyperedge and H′=(V,ℱ∖{e})H^{\prime}=(V,\mathcal{F}\setminus\{e\}). Then clH′​(A)⊆clH​(A)\mathrm{cl}_{H^{\prime}}(A)\subseteq\mathrm{cl}_{H}(A), and the recomputation cost is O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk).

  3. 3.

    Acquisition distance stability. For any g∈Vg\in V, insertion of e=(S,T)e=(S,T) can decrease δ⁡(g,A)\delta(g,A) by at most |T||T|. Deletion can increase δ⁡(g,A)\delta(g,A) by at most |T||T|.

Theorem 11.7 (Safety Under Dynamic Updates).

Let A∈ℛ⁡(F)A\in\mathcal{R}(F) and let e=(S,T)e=(S,T) be a candidate new hyperedge. The post-insertion configuration remains safe—A∈ℛH′​(F)A\in\mathcal{R}_{H^{\prime}}(F)—if and only if clH′​(A)∩F=∅\mathrm{cl}_{H^{\prime}}(A)\cap F=\emptyset, which by Theorem 11.6 reduces to checking whether clH​(A∪T′)∩F=∅\mathrm{cl}_{H}(A\cup T^{\prime})\cap F=\emptyset where T′=T⋅𝟏[S⊆C]T^{\prime}=T\cdot\mathbf{1}[S\subseteq C]. This check costs O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk). A safety monitor for a dynamic agentic system need only run a single incremental closure check per tool addition.

12 Implications for Agentic AI

The hypergraph closure framework provides a mathematical model for modern agentic AI architectures with four key consequences.

Goals are self-consistent.

Every goal in GF​(A)G_{F}(A) is derivable from AA via the hypergraph, eliminating planning failures where agents pursue structurally unreachable goals.

Goals are transparent and auditable.

The derivation certificates provided by the Safe Audit Surface Theorem (Theorem 10.1) make every goal in Emg⁡(A)\mathrm{Emg}(A) and NMFF​(A)\mathrm{NMF}_{F}(A) inspectable and explainable.

Goals are adaptive.

When a tool becomes unavailable or a new API is added, ℱ\mathcal{F} updates and cl⁡(A)\mathrm{cl}(A) is recomputed. Goals relying on a now-absent capability are automatically removed from the reachable set; new goals enabled by the addition appear immediately.

Coalition safety is tractable online.

Theorem 11.2 reduces the safety question for any dynamically forming coalition to a single linear-time query against the precomputed antichain ℬ⁡(F)\mathcal{B}(F).

The deepest implication.

In classical AI, the goal is the starting point and capability is the means. The hypergraph closure inverts this relationship: capability is the starting point, and goals are what the closure reveals. Understanding what a system of agents can become—not just what it currently does—requires reasoning at the level of hypergraph structure, not individual components.

13 Future Research

  • •

    Full live deployment case study. Applying the Safe Audit Surface, coalition criterion, and adversarial robustness check to a production agentic pipeline with independent conjunctive dependency annotation.

  • •

    Tighter PAC bounds. The VC-dimension bound of Theorem 14.2 is not tight for structured hypergraph families. Tighter sample complexity via Rademacher complexity or compression arguments is an open problem.

  • •

    Multi-agent goal discovery. Characterising when coalition formation leads to emergent goals that no individual agent could discover alone.

  • •

    Integration with LLM-based reasoning. Treating a large language model’s function-calling graph as an empirical hypergraph for a practical implementation of the Safe Audit Surface.

  • •

    Approximate safe audit surfaces. Developing tractable approximations to ℬ⁡(F)\mathcal{B}(F) for large-scale deployments where exact coNP computation is infeasible.

14 Further Theoretical Extensions

14.1 PAC-Learning Capability Hypergraphs from Traces

Definition 14.1 (Trajectory and Conjunctive Witness).

A trajectory is a pair (σ,v)(\sigma,v) where σ⊆V\sigma\subseteq V is the set of capabilities active during a session and v∈Vv\in V is a capability observed to fire at its end. A trajectory (σ,v)(\sigma,v) is a conjunctive witness for a candidate hyperedge (S,{v})(S,\{v\}) if S⊆σS\subseteq\sigma and v∉cl1​(σ)v\notin\mathrm{cl}_{1}(\sigma).

Theorem 14.2 (PAC-Learning Sample Complexity).

Let H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}) be an unknown capability hypergraph with |V|=n|V|=n and maximum tail size kk. Let ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} be the hypothesis hyperedge set inferred from mm i.i.d. trajectories by the conjunctive-witness rule. For any ε,δ∈(0,1)\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1),

m≥1ε​(n2​k+ln⁡1δ)m\geq\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(n^{2k}+\ln\frac{1}{\delta}\right)

trajectories suffice to guarantee that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the trajectory sample, the symmetric difference |ℱ​△​ℱ^|/|ℱ|≤ε|\mathcal{F}\triangle\hat{\mathcal{F}}|/|\mathcal{F}|\leq\varepsilon.

Proof.

Model the learning problem as binary classification over the hypothesis class ℋ={(S,{v}):S⊆V,|S|≤k,v∈V∖S}\mathcal{H}=\{(S,\{v\}):S\subseteq V,\ |S|\leq k,\ v\in V\setminus S\}. The number of distinct candidate hyperedges is at most |ℋ|≤n⋅(n−1k)≤n2​k|\mathcal{H}|\leq n\cdot\binom{n-1}{k}\leq n^{2k}. By Sauer’s lemma, the VC-dimension of ℋ\mathcal{H} is at most ⌊log2⁡|ℋ|⌋≤2​log2⁡(nk)\lfloor\log_{2}|\mathcal{H}|\rfloor\leq 2\log_{2}(n^{k}). The standard uniform convergence bound (Blumer et al., 1989) gives m≥1ε​(2⋅VCdim⁡(ℋ)⋅ln⁡(2/ε)+ln⁡(2/δ))m\geq\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(2\cdot\mathrm{VCdim}(\mathcal{H})\cdot\ln(2/\varepsilon)+\ln(2/\delta)), which after absorbing logarithmic factors gives the stated bound. ∎

Remark 14.3.

For the Telco deployment setting of Section 15 (n=12,k=2n=12,k=2), the bound gives m≥1ε​(288+ln⁡(1/δ))m\geq\frac{1}{\varepsilon}(288+\ln(1/\delta)). At ε=0.05,δ=0.05\varepsilon=0.05,\delta=0.05, this requires m≈6,600m\approx 6{,}600 trajectories to learn ℱ\mathcal{F} to 5% error with 95% confidence—well within reach of a production call-centre log.

14.2 Probabilistic Capability Hypergraphs

Definition 14.4 (Probabilistic Hypergraph).

A probabilistic capability hypergraph is a triple Hp=(V,ℱ,p)H_{p}=(V,\mathcal{F},p) where p:ℱ→(0,1]p:\mathcal{F}\to(0,1] assigns to each hyperarc e=(S,T)e=(S,T) a firing probability p⁡(e)p(e)—the probability that ee fires given that all of SS is present. Hyperarc firings are assumed independent.

Theorem 14.5 (Probabilistic Closure).

Let Hp=(V,ℱ,p)H_{p}=(V,\mathcal{F},p) and A⊆VA\subseteq V. Define the expected reachability r(v)=Pr[v∈clp(A)]r(v)=\Pr[v\in\mathrm{cl}_{p}(A)] where clp​(A)\mathrm{cl}_{p}(A) is the random closure obtained by firing each applicable hyperarc ee independently with probability p⁡(e)p(e). Then:

  1. 1.

    r⁡(v)r(v) is computable in O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk) by the probabilistic worklist.

  2. 2.

    The probabilistic safe region ℛp​(F,τ)={A:r⁡(f)≤τ​∀f∈F}\mathcal{R}_{p}(F,\tau)=\{A:r(f)\leq\tau\ \forall f\in F\} is computable in O⁡(|V|⋅(n+m​k))O(|V|\cdot(n+mk)) for any threshold τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1].

  3. 3.

    Non-compositionality persists: there exist A,B∈ℛp​(F,τ)A,B\in\mathcal{R}_{p}(F,\tau) such that A∪B∉ℛp​(F,τ)A\cup B\notin\mathcal{R}_{p}(F,\tau) for any τ<p⁡(h)\tau<p(h) where hh is the unsafe conjunctive hyperedge.

14.3 Adversarial Robustness of the Safe Region

Definition 14.6 (Adversarial Hyperedge Budget).

Given H=(V,ℱ)H=(V,\mathcal{F}), F⊆VF\subseteq V, A∈ℛ⁡(F)A\in\mathcal{R}(F), and budget b≥1b\geq 1, the MinUnsafeAdd problem asks: does there exist a set ℰ′\mathcal{E}^{\prime} of bb new hyperedges such that A∉ℛH′​(F)A\notin\mathcal{R}_{H^{\prime}}(F) where H′=(V,ℱ∪ℰ′)H^{\prime}=(V,\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{E}^{\prime})?

Theorem 14.7 (Adversarial Robustness).
  1. 1.

    MinUnsafeAdd is NP-hard; the single-edge case is decidable in polynomial time (O⁡(n3​k2)O(n^{3}k^{2}) candidates, each checked in O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk)).

  2. 2.

    The robustness ρ⁡(A,F)=min⁡{|ℰ′|:A∉ℛ(V,ℱ∪ℰ′)​(F)}\rho(A,F)=\min\{|\mathcal{E}^{\prime}|:A\notin\mathcal{R}_{(V,\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{E}^{\prime})}(F)\} satisfies ρ⁡(A,F)≥1\rho(A,F)\geq 1 always, and equals 11 iff there exists a candidate hyperedge (S,T)(S,T) with S⊆cl⁡(A)S\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A) and T∩F≠∅T\cap F\neq\emptyset.

  3. 3.

    A greedy defence—choosing at each step the removal of the hyperedge e∈ℱe\in\mathcal{F} that maximises ρ⁡(A,F)\rho(A,F)—achieves a (1−1/e)(1-1/e) approximation to the optimal defensive edge-removal strategy, by submodularity of ρ\rho as a function of ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Proof.

(1) NP-hardness: reduce from SetCover. Given universe UU and sets 𝒮\mathcal{S}, build HH with V=U∪{f}V=U\cup\{f\}, A=∅A=\emptyset, F={f}F=\{f\}, and one candidate hyperedge (Si,{f})(S_{i},\{f\}) per Si∈𝒮S_{i}\in\mathcal{S}. For b=1b=1: iterate over all candidate edges e=(S,T)e=(S,T); if S⊆cl⁡(A)S\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A) and T∩F≠∅T\cap F\neq\emptyset then one edge suffices. There are at most O⁡(n2​k)O(n^{2k}) candidates, giving O⁡(n3​k2)O(n^{3}k^{2}) total.

(2) ρ≥1\rho\geq 1 follows from A∈ℛ⁡(F)A\in\mathcal{R}(F). ρ=1\rho=1 iff a single new edge (S,{f})(S,\{f\}) with S⊆cl⁡(A)S\subseteq\mathrm{cl}(A) reaches f∈Ff\in F directly.

(3) Define g⁡(ℱ′)=ρ⁡(A,F)g(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})=\rho(A,F) under hyperedge set ℱ′⊆ℱ\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F}. Removing an edge from ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} can only increase ρ\rho. The gain g⁡(ℱ′)−g⁡(ℱ′∖{e})g(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})-g(\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\setminus\{e\}) is non-increasing as ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} shrinks, so gg is submodular in the edge set. The (1−1/e)(1-1/e) bound follows from Corollary 8.6. ∎

15 Empirical Validation

The theoretical results make concrete, falsifiable predictions about real agentic pipelines. This section presents validation on 900 trajectories from two independent public benchmarks; the synthetic 500-session illustration in Section 4 is not included in these results.

15.1 Datasets and Protocol

ToolBench G3 (Qin et al., 2023) provides multi-tool agent trajectories spanning 49 API categories (12,657 multi-turn trajectories, 37,204 API calls; Apache 2.0 licence).

TaskBench (Shen and others, 2023) provides task decomposition datasets with explicit tool invocation graphs and human-verified conjunctive dependency annotations; the DAG instances correspond directly to multi-input hyperedges (MIT licence).

For each trajectory, we extract the dependency structure, build both the pairwise graph GG and the capability hypergraph HH, and run all three planners on identical initial capability sets. An AND-violation is recorded when the graph planner fires a conjunctive edge from a partial precondition set that the hypergraph correctly withholds.

Hypotheses.

  • •

    H1: >30%>30\% of multi-tool instances contain at least one conjunctive dependency.

  • •

    H2: Workflow and capability graph planners produce AND-violations at >0%>0\% rate on conjunctive instances; the hypergraph planner produces zero (as proved by Theorem 6.3).

  • •

    H3: Hypergraph closure requires fewer steps than graph BFS on conjunctive instances.

15.2 Results

15.3 Discussion

H1 is confirmed with high confidence: 42.6% of real multi-tool agent trajectories contain conjunctive dependencies. Any system using a pairwise graph model to reason about multi-tool pipelines is misrepresenting nearly half its dependency structure by construction.

H2 is fully confirmed across all three planners. On real asynchronous ToolBench G3 trajectories, the workflow planner produces AND-violations on 38.2% of conjunctive instances (95% CI: [33.4%, 43.1%]) and the capability graph planner on 21.4% (95% CI: [17.3%, 26.1%]). The hypergraph planner produces zero AND-violations on both synthetic and asynchronous data, as guaranteed by Theorem 6.3.

H3 is confirmed with a 1.36×1.36\times efficiency advantage on short chains.

16 Conclusion

This paper introduced capability hypergraphs as a formal framework for modelling compositional AI systems and developed a formal theory of planning, goal discovery, and safety grounded in the closure operator.

The central result is the Non-Compositionality of Safety (Theorem 9.2): the first formal proof that two FF-contained agents can together reach a forbidden goal via an emergent conjunctive hyperedge that neither possesses alone. This result is tight, minimal, and has direct consequences for the design and auditing of modular agentic systems.

The primary deliverable is the Safe Audit Surface Theorem (Theorem 10.1): a polynomial-time-computable, formally certifiable account of every capability an agent can safely acquire from any deployment configuration, what it is one step from acquiring, and what it can never safely acquire.

The complexity landscape is fully characterised: planning is polynomial via Theorem 6.3; emergent capability detection is P-complete (Theorem 8.3); and minimal unsafe set membership is coNP-complete (Theorem 9.5).

Four structural extensions broaden the framework beyond single-agent static systems. The coalition safety criterion (Theorem 11.2) characterises safety for any nn-agent system via a linear-time query against the precomputed minimal unsafe antichain. The incremental closure theorems (Theorems 11.6 and 11.7) reduce per-tool-addition safety monitoring to a single O⁡(n+m​k)O(n+mk) check. The PAC-learning theorem (Theorem 14.2) establishes that the hyperedge structure itself is learnable from trajectory data. The probabilistic extension (Theorem 14.5) shows that non-compositionality persists under stochastic firing, and the adversarial robustness theorem (Theorem 14.7) characterises the complexity of injecting unsafe edges.

Empirically, 42.6% of real multi-tool agent trajectories contain conjunctive dependencies that pairwise graph models cannot faithfully represent. The hypergraph planner produces zero AND-violations across all conditions, as proved by Theorem 6.3.

As AI systems become increasingly modular and compositional, the hypergraph closure framework provides a foundational structure for orchestrating complex agentic behaviour: one in which capability is the starting point, goals are what the closure reveals, and safety is what the structure of FF can certify.
